sections.title: Overview
sections.html:
Overview

Tuberculosis (TB) is a chronic infectious disease caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb), an obligate aerobic, slow-growing acid-fast bacillus transmitted by respiratory aerosols. Although the lungs are the primary site of disease, Mtb disseminates to produce extrapulmonary TB of the lymph nodes, pleura, bones and joints, central nervous system, and genitourinary tract. Infection exists along a spectrum: most immunocompetent hosts contain the bacillus in a clinically silent latent state, while roughly 5–10% progress to active disease, the difference between containment and progression being a property of the host–pathogen interface rather than of the organism alone. The global burden is immense—an estimated 10.8 million people fell ill with TB and 1.25 million died in 2023, and over a quarter of the world’s population carries latent infection.{{cite:who-tb-2024}}

Here, the established etiology is not in dispute: Mtb is the necessary and sufficient cause of TB, and no framework displaces it. What the single-cause model does not explain is the disease’s heterogeneity—why one exposed host clears the bacillus, a second harbors it silently for decades, and a third cavitates and dies. This page reads that heterogeneity through the host metallome, nutritional immunity, and the airway/gut microbiome. The decisive variable is iron. Mtb is an intracellular iron pirate, scavenging host iron through the siderophores mycobactin and carboxymycobactin coupled to the IrtAB importer, all under IdeR control,{{cite:iron-homeostasis}} while the host wages a coordinated counter-campaign—hepcidin-driven hypoferremia, lactoferrin, transferrin, and the siderophore-binding protein siderocalin (lipocalin-2).{{cite:siderocalin}} Macrophage and dietary iron loading consistently track with worse outcomes,{{cite:iron-overload-africa}} and abnormal iron status—at both extremes—independently predicts treatment failure and death.{{cite:iron-status-cohort}}

The metallomic lens reframes care in a direction that matters clinically. Low serum iron in active TB is frequently active host defense—sequestration to starve the bacillus—not a deficiency to be corrected, so reflexive iron repletion can feed the pathogen. The same logic explains a sharp divergence from anaerobe-dominated conditions: because Mtb is an obligate aerobe restricted by granuloma hypoxia, oxygenation strategies such as HBOT are the wrong lever, not a therapeutic one. This page covers, in order: the TB metallomic signature (iron, copper, zinc); the airway and gut microbiome signature along the gut–lung axis; triangle-tested interventions; and explicit STOP recommendations where a conventional reflex would aid the organism.

sections.title: The Causal Chain
sections.html:
The Causal Chain

The metallomic framework resolves TB into an explicit, ordered sequence in which metals act as the selective pressures that decide whether the bacillus is contained or progresses. Mtb supplies the spark; the host metallome and microbiome set the terrain.

  1. The stage is set — exposure meets host iron/redox status and genetics. Inhaled Mtb encounters a host whose baseline iron burden and macrophage genotype are already weighted. Polymorphisms in SLC11A1 (NRAMP1), the phagosomal proton/divalent-cation transporter that moves iron and manganese out of the bacillus-containing vacuole, are reproducibly associated with TB susceptibility (pooled OR ~1.2–1.35).{{cite:nramp1-meta}} High dietary or macrophage iron tilts the terrain toward the pathogen before the immune response even mobilizes.{{cite:iron-overload-africa}}
  2. Phagocytosis and intracellular survival. Mtb is engulfed by the alveolar macrophage but arrests phagosome maturation, establishing a replicative niche inside the very cell meant to destroy it.{{cite:metals-macrophage}}
  3. The iron tug-of-war. Inside the phagosome, Mtb deploys mycobactin/carboxymycobactin siderophores and the IrtAB importer (IdeR-regulated) to strip iron from host stores,{{cite:iron-homeostasis}} while the host counters with hepcidin-driven hypoferremia, lactoferrin, transferrin, and siderocalin (lipocalin-2), which binds carboxymycobactin directly to deny the bacillus its iron-laden chelator.{{cite:siderocalin}} Who wins this exchange is a primary determinant of bacterial load.
  4. Phagosomal metal warfare. The macrophage flips the same metals into weapons, flooding the phagosome with toxic bursts of copper and zinc; Mtb survives only by effluxing them through P-type ATPases (CtpC, CtpV, CtpB), and mutants lacking these pumps are attenuated.{{cite:zinc-poisoning}} Metal intoxication is thus a genuine host defense—and a druggable Achilles’ heel.
  5. Granuloma formation and hypoxia-driven dormancy. Organized immune containment builds the granuloma, whose caseous core becomes hypoxic. Because Mtb is an obligate aerobe, falling O₂ does not aid it—it forces a shift into non-replicating persistence via the DosR/DevR dormancy regulon, the molecular basis of latency and decades-long survival.{{cite:dosr-dormancy}}
  6. Microbiome remodeling along the gut–lung axis. Infection and prolonged antibiotic therapy reshape both the airway and gut microbiota, reducing diversity, impairing epithelial integrity, and amplifying systemic inflammation through bidirectional gut–lung signaling—changes that feed back on immune control, relapse, and recovery.{{cite:gut-lung-axis}}
  7. Outcome. Latent control versus active progression is the settling point of these constraints: ample iron, weak metal intoxication, a permissive NRAMP1 genotype, and a dysbiotic microbiome push toward progression and tissue destruction; effective sequestration, robust Cu/Zn poisoning, and a resilient microbiome favor containment.

The leverage points fall out of the chain itself: do not feed the pathogen’s iron (sequestration is defense, not deficiency); reinforce—never relieve—phagosomal copper/zinc intoxication; respect granuloma hypoxia rather than reversing it; and stabilize the gut–lung microbiome through therapy. Each is examined under the Triangle Test below.
